extracted.intended_audience: readers of political/literary criticism and educated general public interested in colonialism, race, and argument quality
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical literary-criticism essay rebutting James Anthony Froude's claims about the Negro and British colonial policy, focusing on factual accuracy, rhetorical fairness, and moral evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical consistency between premises and strong claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight and challenge internal contradictions in an author's argument (e.g., if the author credits 'accident' or 'natural development' yet makes forcible and confident prophecies about the future).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay points out the inconsistency: if 'accident' alone determines outcomes, firm forecasts are unjustified. Authors should avoid asserting both contingency and deterministic predictions without reconciling them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding racial determinism and epidermal-based authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat skin colour or superficial 'epidermal' traits as grounds for assuming political wisdom or moral authority ('the bidders for predominance over us on the purely epidermal, the white skin, ground, are ipso facto the monopolists of directing wisdom?' ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments must not conflate complexion with capacity; claims that one race is ipso facto wiser must be supported by non-racial evidence, or else rejected as prejudicial generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy about individuals used as exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify the factual status of people cited as examples (e.g., the rebuttal that 'neither Judge Reeves nor Mr. Fred Douglass is a black man' as Froude represented them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on mischaracterized biographies or mis-stated ancestries. When using individuals as evidence, ensure their backgrounds actually match the class or condition being argued about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding false equivalence / ensure comparability of cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not bracket together or compare cases that are not parallel ('the two cases can be distinctly seen to be not in any way parallel').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing lessons from examples, examine social, historical, and institutional context; explicitly justify why cases are comparable before using one to support conclusions about the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and precision in rhetorical framing and tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose wording that accurately reflects reality rather than wishful or misleading phrasing (example: critique of 'should be offered' vs 'are offered').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtle grammatical choices (should/are/will) reveal the author's awareness of facts or desires; careful phrasing is required to avoid masking the present situation or implying facts not true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding cherry-picking and irrelevant/context-dragging
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not boost an argument by dragging in separate contexts or nations (e.g., repeatedly introducing America into arguments about British colonies) when irrelevant, or by selecting atypical examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that cited evidence is representative and relevant to the claim; avoid selective referencing that distorts the broader truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not minimize systemic atrocity via superficial observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using minor social marks (e.g., 'marks of courtesy and good breeding') as justification or exculpation for systemic crimes like slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluation must weigh scale and severity; superficial manners do not neutralize or excuse systemic violence and exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurately represent the composition and real attitudes of communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid misrepresenting the elements and actual attitudes within plural communities ('cardinal dodge ... misrepresenting the elements, and their real attitude towards one another, of the sections composing the British West Indian communities').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When characterizing a multi-ethnic community, account for the diversity of groups and their actual roles—do not invent a homogenous antagonistic bloc for rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sweeping universalizations or overgeneralized claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from broad, absolute phrases that extend a local claim to the entire world ('or anywhere' criticized as 'audacious absurdity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit claims to warranted scope; where generalization is attempted, provide broad supporting evidence rather than extrapolating from narrow cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require evidence for deterministic political causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assert causal inevitabilities (e.g., that giving political power to a certain group 'will' cause societal collapse or slide back) without strong empirical support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political effects are complex and mediated by institutions; avoid simplistic causal narratives that treat single changes (like enfranchisement) as talismans guaranteeing specific catastrophic outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attribute talismanic or magical power to single variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating single factors (a vote, the presence/absence of a class of colonists) as having talismanic virtue that alone produces dramatic social transformations ('What talismanic virtue this prophet ... attributes to a vote').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze multiple causal factors and institutional constraints rather than hinging an argument on a single variable or symbolic act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for differing social and institutional contexts when comparing outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that different polities (e.g., Barbados vs. United States) provide different structures and opportunities, so outcomes for similar individuals may differ ('Most certainly they will, Mr. Froude--but, for the present, only in America, where those opportunities are really free and open to all').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative claims should control for institutional differences, migration patterns, and historical conditions that affect opportunities and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical insinuations or grotesque hypothetical implications without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not imply horrific acts or secret methods (e.g., insinuating organized infant-killing methods) unless supported by evidence; rhetorical questions that suggest atrocities must be responsibly handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careless insinuation distorts debate and may be offensive; where serious allegations are raised, provide substantive proof rather than suggestive rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral framing must reflect the scale and nature of harm rather than social convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject attempts to relativize or exculpate morally reprehensible institutions by appealing to their alleged social utility or survivals from past orders ('Slavery ... IT DOES NOT FOLLOW THAT per se IT WAS A CRIME' challenged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical or functionalist defenses of oppressive institutions should be scrutinized against the lived suffering and systemic harms they produced; moral judgments should not be softened solely by appeals to continuity or custom.
